Teaching Live Edge (Part 3): Mother-Son Collaboration and Practical Joinery

Laura’s finished coffee table in its new home, complete with her dog keeping a watchful eye from the sofa. Each leg was turned into a unique profile as Laura explored the lathe’s creative possibilities—expressing her artistic background through three distinct shapes—before painting them a soft pale gray-blue to complement the rich, golden grain of the Catalpa slab.

When a craft school invites me to teach a woodworking class, the inevitable question always comes up: What skill level is this intended for? Beginners, intermediate, advanced, or somewhere in between?

Because live-edge woodworking can be approached on multiple levels, my answer is almost always inclusive: let everyone in. The joinery can range from straightforward mechanical fasteners to complex cabinetry, but at the end of the day, the live edge itself is the star of the show. The raw beauty of the natural wood grain takes center stage, not an over-engineered carcass or complicated understructure. Knowing this, I know I can coach absolute beginners through the arduous process of flattening a wild slab and then guide them toward a clean, elegant leg construction that matches their abilities.

That philosophy was put into action perfectly by a mother and son who joined us in the studio. Laura, an artist, and her son, Jesse, who was heading off to college at the end of the summer, decided to spend their final weeks together before the transition with a creative retreat on our beautiful campus. Diving into wood—a medium neither of them had ever truly explored—they set out to make something lasting. Despite starting as complete beginners, their finished pieces turned out extraordinary. Both wanted to make a slab: Laura set her sights on a living room coffee table, and Jesse decided to build a sturdy, beautiful bench for the family porch.

Laura and Jesse while sanding their slabs.

After surfacing the slabs—which took both of them about a full day of hard work—we moved on to structuring the bases.

For her coffee table, Laura used a stunning piece of Catalpa—a remarkable wood featuring a rich, golden-brown color and striking grain patterns that you rarely see sitting on standard lumberyard racks. To support it, I proposed using table leg mounting plates (top plates) screwed directly to the underside of the slab, into which table legs are threaded using hanger bolts. It’s a wonderfully strong system, especially for low coffee tables where extra leg rails aren’t required, allowing the natural grain and live edges to remain completely unobstructed.

A bench, however, is a different mechanical animal. Because a bench is subjected to lateral movements and uneven, heavy shifting weights, I advised Jesse that a plate-and-bolt system wouldn’t be ideal. Instead, the best approach was to turn custom tenons on the lathe at the top of each leg and anchor them securely into matching mortises (drilled holes) on the underside of the slab.

Installing a Hanger Bolt into a Turned Leg (A) Drilling a pilot hole into the top of the turned leg to provide proper bite for the hanger bolt’s coarse wood thread. (B) Using the double-nut technique (or a jam-nut driver setup) with a wrench to drive the bolt securely into the end grain. (C) Final assembly showing the leg threaded into a top-mounted plate, with excess thread depth accommodated by a recessed clearance hole bored into the underside of the tabletop.

Both Laura and Jesse dove right in. Laura found working on the lathe exhilarating; it was her first time on a full-scale lathe, and she shaped each of her legs according to a different, custom design.

When it came time to set the anchor bolts into the tops of her turned legs, we used a clever shop trick. While you can drive a hanger bolt by jamming two nuts against each other and turning the top nut with a wrench, we streamlined the process. We jammed two standard mounting plates face-to-face against one another on the bolt threads. Inspired by how smoothly that workflow operated, I quickly grabbed a piece of scrap plywood, cut it into a comfortable handle shape, and screwed one of the mounting plates directly to it. That makeshift handle replaced the top nut in our double-plate setup, giving us massive leverage to drive the anchor bolt home effortlessly. (You can see a demonstration of this in the accompanying video.)

Once Laura finished her legs and installed the anchor bolts, she packed them up to take home, where she painted the legs and screwed them directly into the mounting plates already secured to the underside of her table.

Jesse took a different mechanical route for his porch bench. He shaped his four legs to be square in cross-section, chamfered the corners with a hand plane, and then smoothed them with thorough sanding before mounting them on the lathe just long enough to turn clean, round tenons at the top. After drilling matching holes into the underside of his bench top, he glued the legs firmly into place.

Because he had four solid legs touching the floor, leveling was critical. We placed his completed bench on a flat, reference-leveled surface, slid custom shims underneath any short legs until the benchtop sat perfectly level, and then used a pencil clamped to a fixed-height block to scribe around the bottom of all four legs. That gave us an exact parallel cut line to saw off the excess length. After a final sanding and the application of a protective finish, his bench looked formidable, practical, and deeply authentic—a testament to what first-time makers can achieve in the studio.

 

Yoav Liberman
